newsitem.title: USA: Johnson Controls reaches tentative pact with UAW.
newsitem.headline: Johnson Controls reaches tentative pact with UAW.

text.p: Johnson Controls Inc. said Thursday it reached tentative contract agreements with the United Auto Workers union, ending a 24-day strike that disrupted production of one of Ford Motor Co.'s most profitable vehicles.

The contracts cover about 500 workers at a seat assembly plant in Plymouth, Mich., and another in Oberlin, Ohio. Workers at the plants will be asked to ratify the pacts within two days, the company said. Plans for resuming production will be announced later.

Details were not released, but company officials said the agreements will provide wages and benefits comparable to those at other Johnson Control facilities. Officials said the contracts, the first for the two plants since workers joined the UAW last year, are fair and reasonable in terms of the Johnson Controls' business goals.
A UAW spokesman could not be reached for comment.

The union had been pressing for the company to pledge neutrality in organizing attempts at other plants. Only six of Johnson Controls' 34 U.S. facilities are unionized. But a source close to the strike said the contracts do not include any neutrality language.
Workers went on strike Jan. 28 when talks broke down. The UAW has said it wants base pay levels equal to the $14 to $16 an hour that competitor Lear Corp. pays.

The Plymouth plant employs about 300 hourly workers and produces seating for the Ford Expedition full-size sport utility vehicle. The Oberlin plant employs about 200 hourly workers and produces seating for the Econoline and Club Wagon full-size vans.

In an unprecedented move, Ford refused to accept seats made by non-union replacements. But it continued to build vehicles, believing the strike would be over soon. After making close to 15,000 Expeditions and Econolines without seats, it opted to shut the lines down. Analysts estimate Ford earns about $10,000 in pretax profits on each Expedition.

Expedition production was restarted Feb. 12 with rear seats from Lear. Ford supplied front seats by increasing production at its Chesterfield, Mich., trim plant, which already makes seats for the F-Series pickup trucks. As of Thursday, the company had shipped 1,700 Expeditions to dealers since production was resumed.

Ford spokesman Bert Serre said Thursday that Lear and the Chesterfield facility will continue to assemble seats for the 12,700 Expeditions that have been produced without seats. Once those vehicles are retrofitted, only Johnson Controls will be the Expedition seat supplier, he said.

Serre added Ford has not yet decided when it will resume production at its Econoline assembly line in Lorain, Ohio, and a related frame and paint operation in Avon Lake, Ohio. A total of 2,800 workers are idled at those operations.

Ford's decision to support the union will reverberate in the mostly non-union independent supplier industry, which is under intense pressure from automakers to cut costs, said Donna Parolini, president of International Business Development Corp, a Troy, Mich.-based consultant.
Suppliers now question whether Ford truly wants a partner relationship, a sentiment that could lead to them not bidding on future work, she said.
"Behavior speaks louder than words, and Ford's action said something different than what they've been saying all along," she said.

As part of its interim arrangement, Johnson Controls had moved tooling and equipment for making seat frames out of the Plymouth facility and to a plant in Cadiz, Ky. Company spokesman Jeff Steiner said there were no immediate plans to shift that equipment back to Plymouth. He declined to comment on the employment ramifications of that decision.
Johnson Controls stock gained 50 cents to $85.875 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange. Ford edged up 12.5 cents to $32.875, also on the NYSE.
